strengths: The main contribution is a useful simplification of a difficult geometric estimation problem: generating an approximate virtual correspondence enables reuse of established five-point and P3P solvers. The training-free mean-point variant is particularly accessible. This methodological contribution provides the strongest reason for weak acceptance.

The real-data results support competitive accuracy among dedicated 4p3v methods. Across 10,000 triplets, Table 1 shows that 4p3v(L) improves AUC@5 over homotopy continuation from 43.25 to 47.14 on Sacre Coeur and from 19.45 to 21.34 on St. Peters’ Square. The much simpler 4p3v(M) achieves approximately comparable accuracy to that baseline.

The evaluation includes useful complementary evidence: a study of virtual-point placement, controlled noise experiments, integration into GC-RANSAC, and comparisons with the practical 5pt+P3P baseline. The manuscript clearly explains the overconstrained nature of 4p3v and acknowledges approximation error and the limited practical advantage of dedicated four-point methods.

The learned predictor transfers from entirely synthetic training data to real images. The supplement documents its architecture, loss, and training settings, and provides an additional two-view experiment on 9,900 pairs. That experiment supports some applicability beyond three-view estimation, with the mean-point variant trading a modest accuracy reduction for lower reported runtime.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not fully measure the stated three-camera pose problem. Section 5 scores rotations and normalized translation directions for pairs 1–2 and 1–3, omitting the relative baseline scale. Configurations with incorrect relative camera distances can therefore receive identical scores. The pairwise Sampson scoring also does not constrain this scale. Relative-scale or reconstructed-camera-configuration error would be needed to substantiate complete three-view recovery.

A practical accuracy–runtime advantage over 5pt+P3P is not established. In Table 1, 4p3v(L) has similar accuracy but takes approximately 6–15 times longer, while 4p3v(M) is less accurate at similar runtime. The suggested benefit under heavy outlier contamination is not evaluated through controlled outlier-rate or time-budget experiments. This limits the efficiency claim, although implementation simplicity remains valuable.

The reliability of the approximation is insufficiently characterized. Figure 2 establishes favorable average epipolar error for the sampled distributions, while Figure 3 shows appreciable pose error even without measurement noise. The triangle-based argument supplies no tight accuracy guarantee. Two real landmark scenes and one scene for the noise experiment leave uncertainty about strong perspective distortion, depth variation, and poorly conditioned configurations.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified despite the useful network documentation: RANSAC thresholds and stopping limits, handling of multiple five-point/P3P solutions, and the local-refinement procedure. These choices materially affect both accuracy and runtime. Code and trained models are only promised in the supplied manuscript, so they cannot resolve these omissions in the present assessment.
